title: Cache Preemption Poisoning Attacks on LLM-Based Log Parsers

contributions.purpose: Introduce a new attack vector that exploits the adaptive caching used by LLM-based log parsers.
contributions.mechanism: Define cache preemption poisoning, where an adversary injects crafted log lines that front-load over-generalized templates intercepting later clean logs via prefix-tree matching.
contributions.evaluation: Demonstrated qualitatively on LILAC's prefix-tree cache as an exploitable attack surface created by the efficiency mechanism.
contributions.source_quote: We identify cache preemption poisoning as a novel attack vector against LLM-based log parsers with adaptive caching, demonstrating that the efficiency-enabling cache mechanism creates an exploitable attack surface.

contributions.purpose: Quantify the severity and specificity of the poisoning attack under a small budget.
contributions.mechanism: Inject a 2% poison budget of crafted log lines and compare against random-noise injection.
contributions.evaluation: 2% poison causes catastrophic degradation of -67.17 percentage points in parsing accuracy (PA), with crafted poison over 35x more effective than random noise.
contributions.source_quote: We show that a 2% poison budget causes catastrophic degradation (-67.17pp PA), and that crafted poison is over 35x more effective than random noise, confirming the attack's specificity.

contributions.purpose: Show the attack nullifies the benefit of adaptive caching entirely.
contributions.mechanism: Compare poisoned LILAC against a naive stateless LLM baseline on template accuracy.
contributions.evaluation: Attack pushes LILAC below stateless baseline (56.03% vs 66.67% FTA), negating the advantage of adaptive caching.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that the attack is severe enough to push LILAC below stateless baseline performance (56.03% vs 66.67% FTA), completely negating the benefits of adaptive caching.

contributions.purpose: Provide a partial defense against the attack.
contributions.mechanism: Propose and evaluate a wildcard density screening defense that filters over-generalized poison templates.
contributions.evaluation: Recovers 40.30% of lost PA, while its limitations are identified for future work.
contributions.source_quote: We propose and evaluate a wildcard density screening defense that recovers 40.30% of lost PA, while identifying its limitations for future work.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Among these approaches, LILAC (Jiang et al. 2023a) stands out by combining LLM parsing with an adaptive caching mechanism: parsed templates are stored in a prefix-tree structure that enables efficient retrieval for similar logs, dramatically reducing API calls while maintaining high accuracy.
We identify a novel attack vector—cache preemption poisoning—where an adversary injects a small number of crafted log lines to corrupt the parser's cache state.

Unlike runtime prompt injection attacks that affect individual queries, cache poisoning attacks corrupt the parser's state, causing subsequent clean logs to be misparsed even after the attacker stops injecting malicious content.
